newsitem.title: CHINA: China says Australia pandering to U.S. interests.
newsitem.headline: China says Australia pandering to U.S. interests.

text.p: China on Monday accused Australia of pandering to U.S. interests and warned that aping the United States coupled with anti-Asian sentiment could damage Canberra's relations with Asian nations.
"When the White House launched an air strike on Iraq, Canberra was unusually eager to ape Uncle Sam at every step," the official China Daily said in a commentary.
"Such parrot-like behaviour can only lead to unpopularity in the international community," it said.

Australia's conservative, Liberal-National government has tried to breathe new life into relations with the United States, a traditional ally Canberra says was neglected by the former, Asia-focused Labour government.
"These facts will unavoidably overshadow Australia's Asian foreign policy, making its Asian neighbours hesitant to build further ties with Canberra," the commentary said.
Although Australia had declared it wanted to build ties with Asian neighbours, Canberra had not taken concrete steps to try to improve its standing in the region, it said.

"What countries here have seen instead are cuts in aid and soft loan programmes to this region, and speeches by Australian Parliament member Pauline Hanson full of anti-Asian and anti-immigration sentiment," the commentary said.

Negative publicity over race issues has dogged Canberra since Hanson said in a speech in September that Australia risked being swamped by Asians, and called for an immigration halt to help fight joblessness.
Sino-Australian ties have been strained in recent months by issues such as regional security, Tibet and possible sales of Australian uranium to Beijing's island rival, Taiwan.
Canberra and Washington signed a military pact last July pledging to step up cooperation in regional security issues.
Last month, China angrily denounced a meeting between Australian Prime Minister John Howard and Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, hinting at possible damage to trade relations.
